evals.prompt: I'm DevRel at Tidebreak, we make a Postgres connection pooler. Two of us host, both in Lisbon. Product analytics say 63% of active users are in the US (roughly even East and West), 22% Europe, 9% India, 6% elsewhere. We're going to run a weekly drop-in call. I've pencilled in Wednesdays 15:00 Lisbon because that's 10am New York, which should suit everyone on the US side, and I'll publish it on the community page as '15:00 Lisbon time / 14:00 UTC'. Since Europe is our second biggest group I'm also thinking of adding a European-morning slot on alternate weeks. Can you sanity-check the slot plan?
evals.expected_output: The 15:00 Lisbon slot rejected because US West sits at 07:00, the Lisbon-to-US-East gap computed as 5 hours from Lisbon's own offset, the slot re-anchored in US Eastern with both coasts inside 09:00-18:00 and Lisbon still inside its working day, every region's local time written out, India and the 6% given the async intake as a named path, the slot published in ET with a calendar link and UTC only beside a date, the daylight-saving dates and the one-hour shrink named, the alternate-week European slot refused because 22% sits under the 25% baseline trigger, and one slot plus async intake stated as the default pattern.
expectations: Rejects the 15:00 Lisbon slot because it lands at 07:00 for US West users, outside their 09:00-18:00 working window
Computes the Lisbon-to-US-East gap as 5 hours from Lisbon's own UTC offset rather than reusing the 6-hour Paris figure
Treats the US as the single largest region and anchors the slot in US Eastern time with both coasts inside 09:00-18:00, for example 12:00 ET / 09:00 PT
States that the anchored slot lands at 17:00 Lisbon, inside the hosts' working day, so no late day is needed
Writes the chosen slot's local time for every region in the split: US East, US West, Europe and India
Names India and the 6% elsewhere as the audience outside its working window at that slot and gives them the async intake as a named path rather than the recording alone
Publishes the slot in US Eastern with a calendar link, and gives a UTC time only next to a specific date
Rejects the '15:00 Lisbon time / 14:00 UTC' wording as a slot anchored in host time
Gives the daylight-saving dates: EU on the last Sundays of March and October, US on the second Sunday of March and the first Sunday of November
States that between those dates the Europe-to-US gap shrinks by one hour for two to three weeks in spring and about a week in autumn
Tells them to anchor the slot in the audience time zone and let the hosts' local time move
Refuses the alternate-week European slot now because Europe at 22% sits under the second-slot trigger of 25% of active users, and labels 25% as a baseline
Recommends one slot plus async intake as the default coverage pattern and states the efficiency ordering with it first
Says to poll the audience before fixing the slot and to re-run the regional split after the pilot before adding any second slot

evals.prompt: We're Lanternfold, we shipped the public beta of our event-streaming SDK three weeks ago. I want to launch weekly office hours starting next Thursday to build momentum. So far we have maybe two questions in support and one Discord thread, but that will grow once people hear about the sessions. Staffing is me (DevRel) plus two backend engineers who said they're happy to join when they can. I want to do it as a livestream on YouTube so the recordings pile up as content. Give me the plan.
evals.expected_output: No format proposed before the gating questions; the demand gate applied so every live format is deleted for now and an async intake thread runs first; the livestream deleted for a rotation under three; the cap and the cap arithmetic showing two engineers cannot staff weekly; written manager agreement replacing goodwill; backup host; a six-session pilot with the continue bar written first; recording views refused as a reason to pick the format.
expectations: Declines to propose a format before the gating interview questions are answered, asking them one at a time and multiple-choice where possible
Applies the demand gate: fewer than five questions from the last month that the docs did not answer means every live format is deleted for now
Recommends running an async intake thread first and fixing the docs it surfaces before any live session
Names the plan as the launch-weekly failure pattern: a weekly live slot before anyone has asked anything
Deletes the livestream panel because the rotation holds fewer than three engineers
Applies the engineer cap: at most one session per engineer per month, about 75 minutes each, labelled baseline with Kubernetes' 1 hour per month as the precedent
Does the cap arithmetic: weekly needs about six engineers (sessions per month plus one spare), so two engineers cannot staff it
Rejects engineers who 'said they're happy to join when they can' as a staffing plan and requires written manager agreement with the session counted in their review
Requires a named backup host as well as a host
Requires a pilot of at least six sessions with the continue bar written into the charter before the first session
Refuses recordings piling up as content as a reason to pick the livestream, and counts distinct askers and docs fixes rather than recording views
Stores the interview answers in devrel-context.md or the harness memory system, with a date on task entries
Says which interview answer moved which format option: the demand gate and the rotation size
Keeps async intake in the design whatever live format is chosen later

evals.prompt: Our monthly engineering AMA at Brimwater (feature-flag platform) has been on the calendar four times since June. Askers: June 2, July 1, August 0. September didn't happen, our engineer was out sick and I had nobody else, so the Zoom just sat there. I've posted two write-ups, both about a week after. Zero docs changes came out of it, and the same question about SDK init order keeps coming back. Leadership wants to either kill it or go weekly to build a habit and put it on YouTube so we can report views. I've read that 3 askers per session is the benchmark, so we're clearly under. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: Two bars read separately: the demand bar failing (median askers 1, zero docs fixes) sends the program to an async thread for a quarter with a re-test; the silent cancellation and late write-ups are operating-bar fixes, not stop reasons; weekly refused with slot and promotion changed before cadence; YouTube views refused as viewer vanity; the 3-asker figure relabelled a self-set baseline with no published benchmark; the review brought forward on three sessions under the bar; the backup-engineer rule; a docs ticket on the repeat question; closure protocol if the live session stops.
expectations: Reads two bars separately: a demand bar that decides continue or stop and an operating bar that decides what to fix
Places median askers of 1 and zero docs fixes under the demand bar and recommends dropping to an async thread for a quarter and re-testing demand
Names the silent September cancellation and the late write-ups as operating-bar failures that decide what to fix, never whether to stop
Rejects going weekly, and puts slot and promotion changes before any cadence change
Rejects YouTube views as the reported metric, names it the viewer-vanity failure, and counts distinct askers and docs fixes instead
States that no organization publishes an attendance benchmark for office hours and that 3 askers per cycle is a self-set baseline, not an industry figure
Notes that a monthly program's pilot is two quarters or at least six sessions, and that three sessions under the bar bring the pilot review forward
States the rule the September session broke: the named backup engineer takes it, and a cancellation is announced only when engineer and backup are both out
Gives the write-up deadline as 2 business days (baseline) and marks a week late as a miss
Opens a docs ticket for the repeated SDK init order question because it has been seen more than once
Keeps the same engineer rotation during the async quarter and publishes the repeat answers as docs so the re-test is fair
Gives the closure protocol if the live session stops: a closure post where sessions were announced, a pointer to the async thread, and every calendar entry removed
Labels resulting issues and docs changes (for example 'Office Hours') so the next review can count them

evals.prompt: Writing the rules for our fortnightly developer call at Kelpwire (shipping-rates API, mostly paying customers, plus an enterprise tier on contracts). Draft so far: 'Ask us anything about Kelpwire! No question too small.' Things that happened recently: a customer spent 20 minutes on their invoice dispute; someone showed a way to see another account's rate tables (fixed since); and a dev wants us to walk through their production integration with their logs on screen next time. To prep better I want the question form to ask people to attach logs and config. Sales also asked us to use the slot to talk up what's coming on the Enterprise plan. One enterprise customer wants to bring their custom carrier connector code. Can you write the scope card and the form?
evals.expected_output: A scope card with in-scope and out-of-scope examples in the user's words, each out-of-scope item with a destination: billing to support, the vulnerability to the private disclosure channel never live, live debugging off topic with a minimal reproduction instead, Enterprise roadmap and price refused with only public-docs facts allowed, the contract customer's connector code sent to their account channel, logs and configs removed from the form, the six-field form, recording policy and code of conduct printed on the card, a pinned no-secrets rule with a redaction path, the card read at session open, and the five triage buckets.
expectations: Rejects 'Ask us anything, no question too small' and writes a scope card with three to five in-scope examples phrased as users would ask them and three to five out-of-scope items each with a destination
Routes account, billing and invoice questions to support
Routes a suspected vulnerability to the private security disclosure channel and states it is never raised live or in a public thread
Declares live debugging of a user's own environment off topic under the no-access rule and asks for a minimal reproduction with secrets removed
Routes pricing and Enterprise-tier questions to the sales contact, and limits answers to what the public docs already say about paid features with nothing about roadmap or price
Sends the enterprise customer's custom connector code to their support or account channel under the contract's confidentiality terms, while keeping their public-API how-to questions welcome
Removes logs, configs and screenshots from the intake form and explains they carry secrets and customer data into a tool nobody reviews

Limits the form to six fields: the question, what was tried and which docs page was read, product and version, recording consent (yes / anonymise / write-up only), optional time zone, optional contact with consent to keep the handle on a feature request
Routes a reproducible bug to the issue tracker with an offer to help write the report
Logs feature requests live in the feedback record and says the product team decides
Prints the recording policy and the code of conduct link on the scope card
Pins a 'no logs, keys or customer data' rule at the top of the intake thread and gives moderators a redaction path
Reads the scope card at the start of each session together with the recording notice and the no-live-debugging line
Sorts pre-submitted questions into answer live, answer async, redirect, docs gap and log for product, most widely useful first, and never silently drops one

evals.prompt: At Marrowline we run two things for partners building plugins on our platform: a monthly livestream Q&A and 30-minute booked 1:1 slots with an engineer. I want to record everything, including the 1:1s, and put it all in a training library. We have a lot of German and Dutch partners so I need the GDPR consent wording, can you give me the standard notice other programs use? Last stream our engineer screen-shared the staging dashboard with an API key visible and it's already published. Also my current opener is 'heads up, we're recording, hope that's cool!' Is that enough?
evals.expected_output: Booked slots never recorded; the livestream recorded and captioned with destination, retention and a no-record path announced; the opener rejected as assumed consent and replaced by a notice said twice; no published GDPR template exists and legal review owns the wording; the leaked API key revoked and every screen-share reviewed before publication; policy printed per format on the scope card; compliance ordering with the livestream highest; booked slots kept for plugin authors with a script and ready environment sent ahead; raw log deleted after the write-up.
expectations: Refuses to record the booked 30-minute slots; internal notes only
Keeps the livestream recorded and captioned, with destination and retention announced and a camera-off, chat-only and anonymised-reading path offered
Rejects 'hope that's cool!' as consent assumed with nothing said about where the recording goes
Writes a notice stating where the recording is published, within how many days, how long it is kept and the no-record path, and says it before recording starts and again when it begins
States that no program publishes a GDPR recording notice template and that legal review owns the notice and retention wording for EU attendees
Tells them to revoke the API key shown on the published stream, citing the token-revocation guidance for demo environments
Requires a pre-publication review of every screen-share segment for tokens, keys, internal hostnames and customer names, cut or blurred
Prints the per-format recording policy on the scope card
Gives the compliance-cost ordering with the livestream panel highest and booked slots second
Keeps booked slots as the right format for partners whose questions need their own code on screen
Warns from the discontinued Kubernetes 1:1 Hour that pairs spent the hour choosing tools, and requires a script and a ready environment sent before each booked slot
Honours every 'don't read my name' request from the intake form
Treats async text as its own record and says so on the scope card
Deletes the raw session log once the write-up is published, after copying consented handles onto logged feature requests

evals.prompt: Context: Ossifer, a vector-database startup. The reason we want office hours is to hear product feedback directly from users, product keeps saying they're flying blind. We have 4 backend engineers willing to rotate and 2 DevRel, all in the same time zone as the users. Our forum has about 30 open questions nobody answered properly. My proposal: a biweekly livestream panel with three engineers because it reaches the most people, plus a Discord 'office hours' channel where we promise an answer within an hour during business hours. Rank the options for me.
evals.expected_output: Async intake kept whatever the live format, at most one live format, the four orderings emitted with the compliance tie justified, the drop-in call promoted because the job is product feedback, the Discord queue deleted because no support team owns it, the livestream named as what the order starves with its promotion condition, order-of-magnitude effort per cycle, the demand gate confirmed by the forum backlog, the default stated, the ranking called a default rather than a law, and the biweekly staffing checked against the cap.
expectations: Runs an async intake whatever live format is chosen, and chooses at most one live format
Gives the efficiency ordering: async thread only > drop-in call > livestream panel > booked slots > staffed queue
Gives the value ordering: livestream panel > staffed queue > drop-in call > async thread only > booked slots
Gives the effort ordering: staffed queue > livestream panel > booked slots > drop-in call > async thread only
Gives the compliance-cost ordering and justifies the tie between async thread and staffed queue: both are text posted under published rules with no voice or face recorded
Promotes the drop-in call because the stated job is product feedback, and says that interview answer moved it
Deletes the Discord one-hour-response queue because no support team owns it, naming its effort as a paid support rota rather than a DevRel slot
Names the livestream panel as what the efficiency order starves and gives its promotion condition: drop-in sessions regularly running out of time with a rotation of three or more
Gives order-of-magnitude effort per cycle: drop-in call about half a staff-day, livestream panel about a day, staffed queue a standing job
Confirms the demand gate is met by the roughly 30 unanswered forum questions
States the default of async intake plus drop-in call
Says the ranking is a default rather than a law and re-ranks against what the team already has
Checks biweekly staffing against the cap: two sessions a month plus a spare needs three or four engineers, so the four fit

evals.prompt: We launched weekly office hours at Quenbury (CI/CD product) in July. Five engineers volunteered in the kickoff meeting. By week five it's just me, the only DevRel, on the call, and when an engineer does come it's always Dario, he's done three of the last four. I've been answering the technical stuff myself and escalating in Slack afterwards. Ideas I'm weighing: a $50 gift card per session, making it fully optional so nobody feels pressured, or just running it solo and saying 'ask the engineers' is aspirational. How do I get them back?
evals.expected_output: The goodwill-rotation failure named, gift cards, optional attendance and the solo option refused, a session cap replacing goodwill with Dario flagged over it, the cap arithmetic showing five engineers cannot hold weekly, written manager agreement counted in reviews, a quarter-ahead rotation with a backup per session, a backup host and a separate note-taker, engineers credited by name, the prep brief 48 hours ahead, the next engineer announced by name and area, and engineer sessions tracked per month.
expectations: Names the goodwill-rotation failure: engineers invited in a kickoff and gone by week four or five
Rejects gift cards, optional attendance and the DevRel-solo option, and says a program staffed by DevRel alone becomes a support desk that cannot answer the hard questions
Replaces goodwill with a cap in sessions: at most one session per engineer per month (baseline), about 75 minutes each
Flags Dario at three sessions in four weeks as over the cap
Does the cap arithmetic: weekly needs about six engineers (four sessions a month plus a spare), so five engineers cannot hold weekly, and moves to biweekly or recruits
Requires each engineer's manager to agree to the cap in writing and to count the session as work in their review
Books the rotation a quarter ahead with a named backup per session, the month's spare engineer serving as that backup
Names a backup host so the program does not die on the host's first holiday, and gives note-taking to someone other than the host
Credits the engineer and their team by name in the session and in the write-up, citing Kubernetes thanking donating employers on air
Sends each engineer a prep brief with the pre-submitted questions and the scope card 48 hours before the session
Announces the next engineer by name and area in promotion, because users come for a person who knows their problem
Names the engineer pool as the single point of failure, citing Kubernetes pausing an edition when panelists ran out
Tracks engineer sessions per month in the session log with the target of no engineer over one

evals.prompt: Our Haverlock office hours (we make a secrets manager) are well attended, 6-8 people each month, and the engineers love the conversations. But the questions are repetitive: 'rotation job fails with a lock timeout' has come up at basically every session since March, and 'how do I scope a token to one namespace' twice. After each session I post the Zoom recording link in Discord and that's our record. When someone asks for a feature I say 'noted, I'll pass it on' and ping product. One user asked last week whether her request from May was ever decided and I had no idea. What's the fix?
evals.expected_output: A docs ticket on the second sighting of each question family, the lock-timeout family grouped and sent to the troubleshooting-docs sibling, the recording link rejected as the write-up and replaced by the write-up sections within 2 business days, feature requests logged in the user's words with a consented handle so the asker hears the decision, the raw log deleted, issues labelled, the write-up linked from the next announcement, the measurement target of one docs fix or feedback record per two sessions read as zero, the answer-and-forget failure named, and a separate note-taker.
expectations: Opens a docs ticket the second time a question family appears, in a session or any channel, and groups the lock-timeout variants into one family with each sighting added to its ticket
Routes the lock-timeout family, as an error, to the troubleshooting-docs sibling skill to write the page
Opens a docs ticket for the token-scoping question because it has been seen twice
Rejects a recording link as the write-up and gives the write-up sections: answered, answered here not live, redirected, logged for the product team, docs we are fixing, next session and submit link
Publishes the write-up within 2 business days (baseline) where the intake thread lives
Logs every feature request in the user's words in the team's feedback record, and names 'noted, I'll pass it on' as the lost-requester failure
Copies the asker's handle into the feedback record with their consent so they hear the decision, and traces the May asker's case to its absence
Deletes the raw session log after the write-up is published
Labels resulting issues and docs changes so the pilot review can count them, citing GitLab's 'Office Hours' label
Links the latest write-up in the next announcement and pins the intake thread the moment the write-up is published
Sets the target of at least one merged docs fix or feedback record per two sessions and reads the current value as zero
Names well-attended sessions with no docs change as the answer-and-forget failure: the session is wasted if the same question comes back next month
Assigns note-taking to someone other than the host so a log exists to write up from

evals.prompt: I need the complete office hours program for Driftmark (edge-functions runtime) by tomorrow: twelve months of sessions, who's on each one, the slot, the rules, the metrics. Don't ask me questions, just produce it and I'll fix what's wrong. Also our VP wants a one-off launch AMA for v4 in two weeks, fold that into the program.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to invent twelve months of named sessions, the gating interview asked before any format, the deliverables in order starting with a one-page charter carrying both bars and a six-session pilot, a one-quarter rotation with everything beyond marked provisional, a measurement table reading 'not measured yet', the launch AMA declared outside a standing program and offered only the scope card and room-handling material, and memory storage offered when the capability exists.
expectations: Refuses to invent twelve months of sessions with named engineers, books the rotation one quarter ahead, and marks everything past the pilot as provisional

Asks the gating interview questions (job, five unanswered questions, user regions, staffing with manager agreement, start date and standing versus one-off, recording constraints) before proposing a format, one at a time and multiple-choice where possible
Produces the deliverables in order: charter, slot plan, rotation calendar, scope card, session log and write-up skeletons, measurement table
Writes a one-page charter with job, audience, format, slot, staffing, scope card, recording policy, outputs, pilot dates, demand bar and operating bar
Presents the charter section by section for validation, or, with no validation available, delivers it whole with the open decisions listed at the top
Sets the pilot at a minimum of six sessions and writes the continue bar before the first session
Fills the measurement table with 'not measured yet' rather than invented values

Puts both bars in the charter: the demand bar (askers per cycle, docs fixes plus feedback records per two sessions) and the operating bar (no silent cancellation, no engineer over the cap, write-ups on time in all but one session)
States that the one-off v4 launch AMA is not a standing program, says so, and offers only the scope card and the room-handling material for it rather than folding it into the pilot
Does not count the launch AMA as one of the pilot sessions
Names exactly one primary job in the charter rather than a list
Offers to store the charter, rotation and session log in persistent memory, gated on the capability being available
Asks about customer type, support, sales and security channels, and promotion channels before writing the scope card, because the card needs their destinations

evals.prompt: Pinewake is an open-source workflow engine, I'm the maintainer with two other core devs. We want to start office hours specifically to get more people contributing code: we have 40 'good first issue' tickets nobody picks up. I was going to do a public monthly call where people ask us anything about the codebase, measure success by how many people show up, and record it for YouTube. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Booked pairing slots on starter issues promoted because the job is contributor growth, chosen as the single live format, success measured in first merged contributions rather than attendance, the onboarding path handed to the contributor-onboarding sibling, pairing slots never recorded, a script and ready environment sent ahead, an async intake kept, the cap sizing the slots, a six-session pilot with the bar written first, no published benchmark, and the promotion condition that lifts booked slots from last in the ordering.
expectations: Promotes booked pairing slots on starter issues because the job is contributor growth, and says that interview answer moved the format choice
Chooses booked slots as the single live format instead of adding them beside a monthly public call
Measures first merged contributions per cycle instead of how many people show up
Writes the demand bar in the charter in first merged contributions, with the fallback format named below it
Hands the contributor onboarding path to the contributor-onboarding sibling skill
Never records the booked pairing slots, keeping internal notes only
Sends each participant a script and a ready environment before the slot, citing the discontinued Kubernetes 1:1 Hour where pairs spent the hour choosing tools
Keeps an async intake thread taking questions all week
Caps each core dev at one session per month (baseline) and sizes the bookable slots per month to that cap with one spare
Requires a pilot of at least six sessions with the continue bar written before the first one
States that no organization publishes attendance or repeat-attendance benchmarks for office hours, so any target is self-set
Acknowledges that booked slots rank last on value in the default ordering and names the contributor-growth job as the condition that promotes them
